title: Letters to a friend
hookLine: late in life, Seneca writes 124 letters to Lucilius, a friend in Sicily, about living well

lines: A LETTER WITH YOUR NAME ON IT.
cards: Somewhere in a drawer, a shoebox or an old email account, you may have a letter someone wrote only to you. Not a group message. Not a post.
A letter with your name at the top, written by someone thinking about you as they wrote. Those are the kind people keep.
Long ago, an old and powerful Roman stepped back from public life and started writing letters like that to one friend. People are still reading them.

teach.b: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a well-known writer in Rome. He was exiled, called back, and became tutor and then advisor to the young emperor Nero. He grew very rich.

He lived right in the middle of everything the Stoics warned about, and he knew it. The historian Tacitus tells how he finally asked Nero's leave to withdraw from court, and offered to hand back his wealth.
Lucilius, the letters tell us, was serving as a Roman official in Sicily, a writer himself, interested in philosophy. Seneca writes to him as an equal a few steps behind on the same path.
Every letter opens the same way, in Latin: Seneca to his Lucilius, greetings. A hundred twenty-four survive, written in Seneca's last years.
They're short. Each usually takes something ordinary, a trip, a cold bath, a noisy apartment, a visit to an old house, and turns it into a lesson about how to live.
Readers still argue whether Lucilius really received them all or Seneca wrote them to be published.
Either way, they're written to one person.

Later, Tacitus tells us, Nero accused Seneca of a part in a plot against him and ordered him to die. The letters were written with that shadow already falling, which is why they're urgent and tender at once.
For the next stretch of the path, we'll read them in order, a letter at a time, as if they were addressed to us.

how: Some readers work through Seneca's letters one at a time, a letter a day, and some keep up the habit of writing reflective letters to a friend.

games.q: you're Seneca. you're rich, well-known and at the emperor's side, and it's getting dangerous. what do you do?
o: stay close to Nero and keep advising.
ask to withdraw, and spend your last years writing to a friend.
games.why: Tacitus says he asked to step back from court; in the years left he wrote the letters to Lucilius. later, Nero ordered his death anyway.

practice: Think of one friend you haven't really written to in a while, and picture them at their kitchen table, opening something from you.
In your head or on paper, begin: dear, and their name, then add two or three sentences: something you noticed, something you've been thinking about, something you hope for them.
You don't have to send it; just write to one person, the way Seneca did.

wordCard.voice: Lucilius. The Roman official in Sicily to whom Seneca wrote a hundred twenty-four letters in his last years, each one turning an ordinary day into a lesson about living well.

carryVoice: Your line: dear friend. A letter to one person can still be read two thousand years on. Until the next letter.
